Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/d4/d47102fe8d01acf93fe0e6ef9017e06412e843ea64584b9f4e7151214aeb9197.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x-y+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-y+6\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-y+6\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-y+6\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy+6x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{13}{2}-y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{13}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =y-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}y-x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y-x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =11+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba" :answer-field/id #uuid "f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" "answer-8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" "answer-ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" "answer-022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" :answer/id #uuid "ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer/id #uuid "9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" :answer/id #uuid "8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" :answer/id #uuid "ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5" :answer/id #uuid "022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198628 :question/problem "![](images/6b/6b0c9a89f2768561274d66416b1f5c30fd3fad808ea8d311773fad9272fa1692.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/a9/a900f65b194e7992d3de6abfb078ff0c7cd1e2d163861d9ade810409d632693d.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2+6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2y+3{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2+3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[2z+{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =3+(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194399 :answer-field/correct 17592186194401 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-348cfda2-2f1c-590f-874e-27ed4639164d" :question/id #uuid "348cfda2-2f1c-590f-874e-27ed4639164d" :question/math-academy-id "q-161218" :question/problem "![](images/07/0785d19e62e5b317bbaee924fa8b6b303c2bbd10ab338357e6a88846b1d5b1d1.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/fd/fdaad0039f4b7fea5c6e301f4cc3b89687f5f4081e3bd87f8ce31daacda2744b.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}9-6y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[9y-3{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}9\,\text{d}y \\  & =-9[y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =6+(-18) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bebafe40-b7bb-506e-8e35-eb97971e464b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bebafe40-b7bb-506e-8e35-eb97971e464b" :answer-field/id #uuid "bebafe40-b7bb-506e-8e35-eb97971e464b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b585aa7c-e074-5288-bfb9-ef96a42c4a17" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b585aa7c-e074-5288-bfb9-ef96a42c4a17" "answer-c0eb1d49-0894-5e35-8da8-22eace89ec4e" "answer-cda7553e-81c6-5b0b-b7ee-b9649cfb537a" "answer-c0ddf932-21f8-5717-80af-819313ab65be" "answer-2b26cc63-426c-571e-9b86-42c72dd116be"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b585aa7c-e074-5288-bfb9-ef96a42c4a17" :answer/id #uuid "b585aa7c-e074-5288-bfb9-ef96a42c4a17" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0eb1d49-0894-5e35-8da8-22eace89ec4e" :answer/id #uuid "c0eb1d49-0894-5e35-8da8-22eace89ec4e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cda7553e-81c6-5b0b-b7ee-b9649cfb537a" :answer/id #uuid "cda7553e-81c6-5b0b-b7ee-b9649cfb537a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0ddf932-21f8-5717-80af-819313ab65be" :answer/id #uuid "c0ddf932-21f8-5717-80af-819313ab65be" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b26cc63-426c-571e-9b86-42c72dd116be" :answer/id #uuid "2b26cc63-426c-571e-9b86-42c72dd116be" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-886facf5-e284-5b49-82f5-9671e671cb20" :question/id #uuid "886facf5-e284-5b49-82f5-9671e671cb20" :question/math-academy-id "q-162561" :question/problem "![](images/aa/aac27058402f89bef73700129a7812b3cf4f971c11975fc1711a46b8d10e61fe.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/e2/e2d914cf61af684d1f2971ec680acc1a2a53a6a40c85e387728dfea8ebc94730.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-2+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x+2{z}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(2{z}^{2}-2)x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{z}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(x+2{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(x+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2x{z}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(\frac{3}{2}+18) \\  & =-\frac{39}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{27}{2}+(-\frac{39}{2}) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}

Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/8e/8ed6ffdeab54bc6888d245ef4f1c050c31e010c67dfa93aea365fc6cb523e382.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+y-4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+y-4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y-4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy-4x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y-3\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-3y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}2x+y\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+(-\frac{15}{2}) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-723cf9c2-2b81-5164-9613-762892b1d534"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-723cf9c2-2b81-5164-9613-762892b1d534" :answer-field/id #uuid "723cf9c2-2b81-5164-9613-762892b1d534" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ddfc6802-b302-519c-b456-4ec4b85afbc7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ddfc6802-b302-519c-b456-4ec4b85afbc7" "answer-b7b67ca6-6357-50a6-8510-6325cf38d5b8" "answer-06134337-3698-5e99-b304-3c524f8d58ba" "answer-e104162b-8025-5219-bed4-9b1e8c92a728" "answer-d03aaa3c-1379-5383-ba5a-20ab61ae0bbe"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ddfc6802-b302-519c-b456-4ec4b85afbc7" :answer/id #uuid "ddfc6802-b302-519c-b456-4ec4b85afbc7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b7b67ca6-6357-50a6-8510-6325cf38d5b8" :answer/id #uuid "b7b67ca6-6357-50a6-8510-6325cf38d5b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-06134337-3698-5e99-b304-3c524f8d58ba" :answer/id #uuid "06134337-3698-5e99-b304-3c524f8d58ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e104162b-8025-5219-bed4-9b1e8c92a728" :answer/id #uuid "e104162b-8025-5219-bed4-9b1e8c92a728" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{14}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d03aaa3c-1379-5383-ba5a-20ab61ae0bbe" :answer/id #uuid "d03aaa3c-1379-5383-ba5a-20ab61ae0bbe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{19}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-541f1701-1958-5d60-973d-d311e60b511f" :question/id #uuid "541f1701-1958-5d60-973d-d311e60b511f" :question/math-academy-id "q-162541" :question/problem "![](images/58/581ac462bfcfead22a6c5ad4eb247f05adb1a677e92cac51954b0746cd083ab7.png)

$$

$$

{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨8{x}^{2}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨8({1}^{2})({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =8{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(y,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}8{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =8{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =64\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨8({0}^{2})({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =64\pi +0 \\  & =64\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f747b354-6e66-5b1a-8d1f-bb7fe1e6ed70"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f747b354-6e66-5b1a-8d1f-bb7fe1e6ed70" :answer-field/id #uuid "f747b354-6e66-5b1a-8d1f-bb7fe1e6ed70" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-684630f4-73ec-5717-89dc-735d07771dcf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fc5fd008-10bd-5ee2-bb11-b1004b46b242" "answer-e7b2f4d8-a73a-5078-92cb-e52bc18e91d3" "answer-dd410492-acca-5af4-b697-930048beeb2a" "answer-684630f4-73ec-5717-89dc-735d07771dcf" "answer-24e66adf-5d3d-50f8-bd05-476213ea7079"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc5fd008-10bd-5ee2-bb11-b1004b46b242" :answer/id #uuid "fc5fd008-10bd-5ee2-bb11-b1004b46b242" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7b2f4d8-a73a-5078-92cb-e52bc18e91d3" :answer/id #uuid "e7b2f4d8-a73a-5078-92cb-e52bc18e91d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "27\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dd410492-acca-5af4-b697-930048beeb2a" :answer/id #uuid "dd410492-acca-5af4-b697-930048beeb2a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-684630f4-73ec-5717-89dc-735d07771dcf" :answer/id #uuid "684630f4-73ec-5717-89dc-735d07771dcf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "64\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-24e66adf-5d3d-50f8-bd05-476213ea7079" :answer/id #uuid "24e66adf-5d3d-50f8-bd05-476213ea7079" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "81\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ec4a413a-1560-589f-a588-2fce65f680ae" :question/id #uuid "ec4a413a-1560-589f-a588-2fce65f680ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-162539" :question/problem "![](images/14/14b1144f52dcacc094901a159bf54c04f00daccc85df7b117b2163ed327dcd4f.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/61/614037b52ca1f60f03420019891af1004227e2e0f3b4a89d71adbdc68dadf1dd.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(y,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{D}r\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨0\sqrt{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-83518110-ea5d-5b6c-8080-6f96a5271b8b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-83518110-ea5d-5b6c-8080-6f96a5271b8b" :answer-field/id #uuid "83518110-ea5d-5b6c-8080-6f96a5271b8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-253e9383-49a8-53b0-8d24-6a8dbb0d3f09" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc8b366c-7b46-5852-bf2e-27c619fddf3e" "answer-8086102a-b853-545f-8109-277022565d26" "answer-253e9383-49a8-53b0-8d24-6a8dbb0d3f09" "answer-f04bf4db-8996-5572-9ef9-fba37950252e" "answer-84710785-2a7f-5147-a528-99d84da23127"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc8b366c-7b46-5852-bf2e-27c619fddf3e" :answer/id #uuid "bc8b366c-7b46-5852-bf2e-27c619fddf3e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8086102a-b853-545f-8109-277022565d26" :answer/id #uuid "8086102a-b853-545f-8109-277022565d26" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-253e9383-49a8-53b0-8d24-6a8dbb0d3f09" :answer/id #uuid "253e9383-49a8-53b0-8d24-6a8dbb0d3f09" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f04bf4db-8996-5572-9ef9-fba37950252e" :answer/id #uuid "f04bf4db-8996-5572-9ef9-fba37950252e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84710785-2a7f-5147-a528-99d84da23127" :answer/id #uuid "84710785-2a7f-5147-a528-99d84da23127" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7ea6dcfa-a1e9-5981-812c-443a861d4f35" :question/id #uuid "7ea6dcfa-a1e9-5981-812c-443a861d4f35" :question/math-academy-id "q-161234" :question/problem "![](images/e6/e6c13f4405c407123973c370a20c88b9c989bd54ade909b06414eabc22f0d45e.png)

Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=1.$ Therefore,

$$
n=⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3x+4y,\,3y-4x,\,3z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =x(3x+4y)+y(3y-4x)+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2}+4xy+3{y}^{2}-4xy+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}3\,\text{d}S \\  & =3{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =3\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =3\cdot 4\pi \cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =12\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590" :answer-field/id #uuid "a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" "answer-4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" "answer-c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" "answer-8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" "answer-d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer/id #uuid "4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" :answer/id #uuid "4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" :answer/id #uuid "c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" :answer/id #uuid "8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026" :answer/id #uuid "d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9c176acf-06da-52d5-8022-73333152fefe" :question/id #uuid "9c176acf-06da-52d5-8022-73333152fefe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161231" :question/problem "![](images/e7/e73d17583a6aa15601abd957f25cfb11ded37159649a67c5b237915d03ed98f7.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $2$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=2.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x(x-z)+{y}^{2}+z(z+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-xz+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+xz) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 4\pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}

Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=2.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x-3z,\,y,\,z+3x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨x-3z,\,y,\,z+3x⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x(x-3z)+{y}^{2}+z(z+3z)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-3xz+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+3xz) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 4\pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-017293d9-a2de-5bf2-b2b9-63c72dc5e9c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-017293d9-a2de-5bf2-b2b9-63c72dc5e9c4" :answer-field/id #uuid "017293d9-a2de-5bf2-b2b9-63c72dc5e9c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f7b91439-9a71-53df-96c8-314232b56478" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f82b5eab-7255-5b1f-b41e-fa0214204617" "answer-19ccd5aa-3240-5023-a265-5b3b645f65d1" "answer-f7b91439-9a71-53df-96c8-314232b56478" "answer-6ab44418-4fde-5e9e-8a7f-72d3ba9e3f25" "answer-9c5f2113-e26c-58e1-947e-c0300530087b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f82b5eab-7255-5b1f-b41e-fa0214204617" :answer/id #uuid "f82b5eab-7255-5b1f-b41e-fa0214204617" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-19ccd5aa-3240-5023-a265-5b3b645f65d1" :answer/id #uuid "19ccd5aa-3240-5023-a265-5b3b645f65d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f7b91439-9a71-53df-96c8-314232b56478" :answer/id #uuid "f7b91439-9a71-53df-96c8-314232b56478" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6ab44418-4fde-5e9e-8a7f-72d3ba9e3f25" :answer/id #uuid "6ab44418-4fde-5e9e-8a7f-72d3ba9e3f25" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9c5f2113-e26c-58e1-947e-c0300530087b" :answer/id #uuid "9c5f2113-e26c-58e1-947e-c0300530087b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\pi \sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198603 :question/problem "![](images/e6/e6c13f4405c407123973c370a20c88b9c989bd54ade909b06414eabc22f0d45e.png)

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=1.$ Therefore,

$$
n=⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\text{Area}(S) \\  & =4\pi \cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}

For closed surfaces, the convention is the positive orientation is always given by the *outward-pointing* unit normal vector.

![](images/d2/d2bb07e4684cfc3a8c5641ecc6930dbc1c76027a735c7efe0c1c60cd17a91060.png)

 

When calculating the flux of a vector field $\mathbf F$ across a closed surface, we always measure the flux relative to the surface's positive orientation.  

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199469 :tutorial/content "![](images/d2/d2a5641e502b11cca4f469ec743adc62d614f669d61c1b2d0b0c7549fb60bf6b.png)

 

Given a sphere of radius $r$ centered at the origin, an outward-pointing unit normal vector to the sphere at the point $P(x,y,z)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can sometimes use this to calculate the flux of a vector field through a sphere. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198493 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/d4/d47102fe8d01acf93fe0e6ef9017e06412e843ea64584b9f4e7151214aeb9197.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x-y+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-y+6\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-y+6\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-y+6\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy+6x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{13}{2}-y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{13}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =y-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}y-x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y-x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =11+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba" :answer-field/id #uuid "f1c5df89-0a4d-58f0-9562-de84c7296eba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" "answer-8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" "answer-ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" "answer-022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" :answer/id #uuid "ee6f293e-ee33-59bc-ae0a-421d6d6069d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer/id #uuid "9c7f4c11-cb48-56a3-a231-fbfe74c38e3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" :answer/id #uuid "8e594166-996a-561a-a110-dc2f02ae4841" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" :answer/id #uuid "ba1cead4-2415-5cbb-975a-9e945db0ce69" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5" :answer/id #uuid "022cc252-1b2d-53c8-b8f4-7e0fa0c560d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198628 :question/problem "![](images/6b/6b0c9a89f2768561274d66416b1f5c30fd3fad808ea8d311773fad9272fa1692.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/a9/a900f65b194e7992d3de6abfb078ff0c7cd1e2d163861d9ade810409d632693d.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2+6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2y+3{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2+3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[2z+{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =3+(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/e2/e2d914cf61af684d1f2971ec680acc1a2a53a6a40c85e387728dfea8ebc94730.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-2+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x+2{z}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(2{z}^{2}-2)x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{z}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(x+2{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(x+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2x{z}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(\frac{3}{2}+18) \\  & =-\frac{39}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{27}{2}+(-\frac{39}{2}) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-916a132b-ef75-5ddf-ad1d-ae5149411e03"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-916a132b-ef75-5ddf-ad1d-ae5149411e03" :answer-field/id #uuid "916a132b-ef75-5ddf-ad1d-ae5149411e03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6747bbec-720b-52e6-99cc-9d109af4dc8a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c158a00f-6972-5251-9b09-b9f5fb43ebc0" "answer-184fb30f-a682-5501-8386-eb41dfbe9220" "answer-6747bbec-720b-52e6-99cc-9d109af4dc8a" "answer-ffe5a674-7ecb-5030-bc4c-bee02665aeb3" "answer-fed859a1-00f2-56ee-a80c-c935c99c8ac8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c158a00f-6972-5251-9b09-b9f5fb43ebc0" :answer/id #uuid "c158a00f-6972-5251-9b09-b9f5fb43ebc0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-184fb30f-a682-5501-8386-eb41dfbe9220" :answer/id #uuid "184fb30f-a682-5501-8386-eb41dfbe9220" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6747bbec-720b-52e6-99cc-9d109af4dc8a" :answer/id #uuid "6747bbec-720b-52e6-99cc-9d109af4dc8a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffe5a674-7ecb-5030-bc4c-bee02665aeb3" :answer/id #uuid "ffe5a674-7ecb-5030-bc4c-bee02665aeb3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fed859a1-00f2-56ee-a80c-c935c99c8ac8" :answer/id #uuid "fed859a1-00f2-56ee-a80c-c935c99c8ac8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b265113a-f521-5f72-933b-1132d7a6f831" :question/id #uuid "b265113a-f521-5f72-933b-1132d7a6f831" :question/math-academy-id "q-161220" :question/problem "![](images/e8/e8708a16a0f6db347acf2c1a82a602d2fa8ce60d4bb8369f1414eca3465e4e71.png)

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨(3-x){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/00/0072a53c42916c095c625cebd0a0564b92dcac5469f9d7452e9c75ef7e7d7158.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=3$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨(3-3){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨(3-x){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨(3-0){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-3{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-3{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/51/5193451b39b03b11cf9780fd7039360ba8fb5de5876a3593f7a5dadde2e7be5b.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-1}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-0}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-2\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+(-8\pi ) \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-919ef9fd-60f6-5c91-983a-1dea7afd83ed"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-919ef9fd-60f6-5c91-983a-1dea7afd83ed" :answer-field/id #uuid "919ef9fd-60f6-5c91-983a-1dea7afd83ed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1a03aa61-a6a4-59bd-9047-ec009e7bb552" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1a03aa61-a6a4-59bd-9047-ec009e7bb552" "answer-f5a70d9b-245d-5412-9927-59ddc777a811" "answer-08051b4d-e523-5380-b21a-12e9c0665d2c" "answer-0ce314fb-b190-50fc-b3d0-c8253bbb95a3" "answer-a7023940-c9dc-5a8b-a379-2f0028725950"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a03aa61-a6a4-59bd-9047-ec009e7bb552" :answer/id #uuid "1a03aa61-a6a4-59bd-9047-ec009e7bb552" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f5a70d9b-245d-5412-9927-59ddc777a811" :answer/id #uuid "f5a70d9b-245d-5412-9927-59ddc777a811" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-08051b4d-e523-5380-b21a-12e9c0665d2c" :answer/id #uuid "08051b4d-e523-5380-b21a-12e9c0665d2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0ce314fb-b190-50fc-b3d0-c8253bbb95a3" :answer/id #uuid "0ce314fb-b190-50fc-b3d0-c8253bbb95a3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a7023940-c9dc-5a8b-a379-2f0028725950" :answer/id #uuid "a7023940-c9dc-5a8b-a379-2f0028725950" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-74852653-8123-54e4-8cee-cb7081e03f55" :question/id #uuid "74852653-8123-54e4-8cee-cb7081e03f55" :question/math-academy-id "q-162542" :question/problem "![](images/4a/4af0d5c96e08d87ea884ec1f0d5c87e0ca220c54c2783fb299c100cad6582088.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3x+4y,\,3y-4x,\,3z⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $1$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=1.$ Therefore,

$$
n=⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3x+4y,\,3y-4x,\,3z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =x(3x+4y)+y(3y-4x)+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2}+4xy+3{y}^{2}-4xy+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}3\,\text{d}S \\  & =3{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =3\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =3\cdot 4\pi \cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =12\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590" :answer-field/id #uuid "a4c323a0-5a8f-5466-a1d8-57f7d5162590" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" "answer-4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" "answer-c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" "answer-8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" "answer-d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer/id #uuid "4b538de2-0bf9-52bf-9303-9311b62ebd0c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" :answer/id #uuid "4a77d700-dee1-58de-add2-b15b7a553b7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" :answer/id #uuid "c4df7c45-b2ce-53b1-a841-5b246b8afa77" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" :answer/id #uuid "8dd5c682-fccc-58c8-80e3-11d1729f0473" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026" :answer/id #uuid "d97a866d-566f-5022-aaa9-aa18fc519026" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9c176acf-06da-52d5-8022-73333152fefe" :question/id #uuid "9c176acf-06da-52d5-8022-73333152fefe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161231" :question/problem "![](images/e7/e73d17583a6aa15601abd957f25cfb11ded37159649a67c5b237915d03ed98f7.png)

$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$

$$

$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=1.$ Therefore,

$$
n=⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\text{Area}(S) \\  & =4\pi \cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194249 :answer-field/correct "answer-04de0393-ca1b-597d-bacc-969f4123ee27" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0ba5ee31-bb54-534a-8802-752dbe4f750e" "answer-04de0393-ca1b-597d-bacc-969f4123ee27" "answer-de192a5a-1b51-5a1a-836f-190f1c9b7ca4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0ba5ee31-bb54-534a-8802-752dbe4f750e" :answer/id #uuid "0ba5ee31-bb54-534a-8802-752dbe4f750e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-04de0393-ca1b-597d-bacc-969f4123ee27" :answer/id #uuid "04de0393-ca1b-597d-bacc-969f4123ee27" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-de192a5a-1b51-5a1a-836f-190f1c9b7ca4" :answer/id #uuid "de192a5a-1b51-5a1a-836f-190f1c9b7ca4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199479 :tutorial/content "Similar to the case of *closed* curves, there is always a well-defined notion of "inside" and "outside" a closed *surface*. 

For closed surfaces, the convention is the positive orientation is always given by the *outward-pointing* unit normal vector.

![](images/d2/d2bb07e4684cfc3a8c5641ecc6930dbc1c76027a735c7efe0c1c60cd17a91060.png)

 

When calculating the flux of a vector field $\mathbf F$ across a closed surface, we always measure the flux relative to the surface's positive orientation.  

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199469 :tutorial/content "![](images/d2/d2a5641e502b11cca4f469ec743adc62d614f669d61c1b2d0b0c7549fb60bf6b.png)

 

Given a sphere of radius $r$ centered at the origin, an outward-pointing unit normal vector to the sphere at the point $P(x,y,z)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can sometimes use this to calculate the flux of a vector field through a sphere. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198493 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-5dff93a1-4655-5852-a4ef-0e50149062ad" :question/id #uuid "5dff93a1-4655-5852-a4ef-0e50149062ad"] ["question-5dff93a1-4655-5852-a4ef-0e50149062ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-161217"] ["question-5dff93a1-4655-5852-a4ef-0e50149062ad" :question/problem "![](images/83/838fe13d4ad778c391ff628b508d17ed450b56e800180c946038be1ccfc5655e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$"] ["question-5dff93a1-4655-5852-a4ef-0e50149062ad" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/d4/d47102fe8d01acf93fe0e6ef9017e06412e843ea64584b9f4e7151214aeb9197.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x-y+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-y+6\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-y+6\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-y+6\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy+6x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{13}{2}-y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{13}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y+2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =y-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}y-x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y-x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2+6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2y+3{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2+3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[2z+{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/fd/fdaad0039f4b7fea5c6e301f4cc3b89687f5f4081e3bd87f8ce31daacda2744b.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}9-6y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[9y-3{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}9\,\text{d}y \\  & =-9[y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =6+(-18) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-348cfda2-2f1c-590f-874e-27ed4639164d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bebafe40-b7bb-506e-8e35-eb97971e464b" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/e2/e2d914cf61af684d1f2971ec680acc1a2a53a6a40c85e387728dfea8ebc94730.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-2+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x+2{z}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(2{z}^{2}-2)x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{z}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(x+2{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(x+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2x{z}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(\frac{3}{2}+18) \\  & =-\frac{39}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{27}{2}+(-\frac{39}{2}) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-886facf5-e284-5b49-82f5-9671e671cb20" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-916a132b-ef75-5ddf-ad1d-ae5149411e03" :answer-field/id #uuid Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$"] ["question-b265113a-f521-5f72-933b-1132d7a6f831" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/8e/8ed6ffdeab54bc6888d245ef4f1c050c31e010c67dfa93aea365fc6cb523e382.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+y-4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+y-4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y-4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy-4x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y-3\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-3y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}2x+y\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+(-\frac{15}{2}) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b265113a-f521-5f72-933b-1132d7a6f831" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-723cf9c2-2b81-5164-9613-762892b1d534" :answer-field/id #uuid Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$"] ["question-541f1701-1958-5d60-973d-d311e60b511f" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨(3-x){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/00/0072a53c42916c095c625cebd0a0564b92dcac5469f9d7452e9c75ef7e7d7158.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=3$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨(3-3){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨(3-x){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨(3-0){e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-3{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-3{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(y,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =-3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{r}^{2}}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-6\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1) \\  & =3\pi (1-{e}^{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+3\pi (1-{e}^{4}) \\  & =3\pi (1-{e}^{4}).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-541f1701-1958-5d60-973d-d311e60b511f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-77e0a989-8025-59cd-b463-0e58f6dbbcd2" :answer-field/id #uuid Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-1}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-0}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-2\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+(-8\pi ) \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0aa0eff9-8245-5a13-9648-df63821931fe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-919ef9fd-60f6-5c91-983a-1dea7afd83ed" :answer-field/id #uuid
